content: The majority of adverse events (AEs) associated with the use of medical devices for male circumcision are classified as mild or moderate in severity. However, further evidence is required to evaluate the safety benefits of the no-flip collar clamp method, particularly for adolescents, as well as the use of topical anesthesia in these procedures. The elastic collar compression method carries a higher risk of tetanus, necessitating pre-procedure vaccination to mitigate this risk. This requires additional healthcare visits prior to the circumcision procedure. Device-based circumcision methods occasionally result in complications such as device displacement or slippage. These events may necessitate immediate or urgent surgical intervention to prevent serious long-term outcomes. Therefore, healthcare providers performing these procedures must possess the requisite surgical skills to address such complications promptly. Healing times for circumcision performed using in situ devices are typically one to two weeks longer than those for conventional surgical circumcision, due to secondary intention healing. This extended healing period necessitates a longer duration of sexual abstinence or conscientious condom use until the wound has fully healed. Mandatory follow-up visits associated with device-based circumcision methods may potentially reduce their acceptability, although evidence on this issue remains limited. In many settings, voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) is provided to younger adolescents as part of HIV prevention efforts. To maintain effective HIV prevention coverage, programs must determine the appropriate age range to target. The reduction in HIV risk is consistent across all circumcised males, regardless of the age at which the procedure is performed. However, circumcising boys aged 10–14 in high HIV prevalence settings will avert future HIV and STI infections but will not provide immediate benefits if the individual is not yet sexually active. Adolescents’ capacity to provide informed consent varies. While most adolescents aged 15 and older are generally capable of giving informed consent, younger adolescents (ages 10–14) may require case-by-case assessments to determine their ability to consent. As a general principle, non-emergency, invasive, and irreversible interventions should be postponed until the child is sufficiently mature to provide informed consent. National laws or regulations should establish a minimum permissible age for consent to VMMC or provide guidelines for assessing the evolving capacity of individual children. VMMC services must ensure the lowest possible risk of adverse events. Limited evidence suggests that younger adolescents (ages 10–14) undergoing conventional surgical circumcision may experience a higher rate of certain rare but serious adverse events, such as glans injury and urethral fistula, compared to older adolescents. Circumcision for adolescents with immature genitalia should be deferred until they are more physically developed, as male genital growth is typically complete by age 15. VMMC programs present an opportunity to integrate other health interventions, such as comprehensive sexuality education and recommended vaccinations (e.g., tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines). However, the feasibility of offering these services at specific adolescent ages, followed by the surgical procedure at a later age, remains uncertain. Healthcare workers serving adolescent boys should possess the technical competence to provide adolescent-friendly health services, protect adolescents’ rights to information, privacy, and confidentiality, and adopt non-discriminatory and respectful attitudes. They should also receive training on assessing adolescents’ capacity to consent, engaging parents in the informed consent process, and addressing age-specific developmental and physical considerations. Efforts to enhance the uptake of VMMC among adult men and adolescents should focus on addressing barriers to service access and acceptability. Strategies include reorienting services to a more people-centered approach, improving the quality and safety of services, and integrating VMMC into a broader package of health services relevant to men’s life course and health needs. Economic compensation, such as food, transportation, or subsidized vouchers, has been shown to increase VMMC uptake among adult men. However, compensation alone may not address supply-side issues or ensure sustainability. Decisions regarding the use, type, and amount of compensation should involve community engagement and consider the specific context. To close gaps in men’s health and services, it is essential to develop policies and programs that address gender norms, improve men’s access to healthcare, and tackle structural drivers of poor health outcomes. Interventions should be tailored to the specific needs and contexts of target populations, with a focus on enhancing service quality, accessibility, and acceptability.
